title: How endurance performance falls with age
goal: Describe how endurance performance falls with age, how lifelong exercisers compare with sedentary peers, and judge the limits of the evidence.

steps.title: The shape of the fall
steps.text:
Endurance performance does not fall in a straight line. Peak running performance holds until about age 35, eases modestly until 50–60, then falls more steeply [[c:curve]]. [Age-group records](g:age-group-record) show how much stays: in the marathon, athletes over 70 have beaten the winning time of the first modern Olympic Games, in 1896 [[c:records]].

The fall also depends on the sport. Declines in cycling are smaller than in running and swimming [[c:sport]].

These are patterns across groups, not a forecast for one person. Records show what the best can do, not what a typical masters athlete does.

claims.text: Peak endurance running performance holds until about age 35, falls modestly until 50–60, then more steeply.

evidence.quote: Peak endurance performance is maintained until approximately 35 years of age, followed by modest decreases until 50-60 years of age, with progressively steeper declines thereafter.

claims.text: Masters runners over 70 have run marathons faster than the 1896 Olympic winning time.

evidence.quote: In some athletic events (e.g. marathon running), Masters athletes over 70 years of age have surpassed the winning time at the first Olympic games held in Athens

claims.text: Age-related declines in performance are smaller in cycling than in running and swimming.

evidence.quote: smaller age-related declines in cycling performance than in running and swimming have been documented

steps.title: Lifelong exercisers and their peers
steps.text:
What do decades of training buy? Researchers compared men in their 70s who had exercised about 5 days a week for 52 years with healthy non-exercisers of the same age, and with young exercisers, all on [VO₂max](g:vo2max) [[c:gries-vo2]].

| group (men) | VO₂max, mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| young exercisers, 25 y | 53 |
| [lifelong exercisers](g:lifelong-exerciser), 74 y | 34 |
| non-exercisers, 75 y | 22 |

Women show the same order: 44, 26 and 18. In the thigh muscle, lifelong exercisers kept the capillaries and aerobic enzymes of young people [[c:gries-muscle]]. So training buys a lot, but not everything: they still sat well below the young.

claims.text: In lifelong exercisers aged about 74, VO₂max was between that of young exercisers and healthy non-exercisers, in men and in women.

evidence.quote: had a hierarchical pattern (YE > LLE > OH, P < 0.05) for women (44 ± 2 > 26 ± 2 > 18 ± 1 ml·kg-1·min-1) and men (53 ± 3 > 34 ± 1 > 22 ± 1 ml·kg-1·min-1)

claims.text: Over 50 years of aerobic exercise fully preserved capillarization and aerobic enzymes in thigh muscle.

evidence.quote: 50+ years of aerobic exercise fully preserved capillarization and aerobic enzymes, regardless of intensity

steps.title: A percent difference needs the right base
steps.problem: In the same study, performance-trained lifelong exercisers (men) had a VO₂max of 38 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and fitness-trained ones 27. How much higher is the first group?
steps: Divide by the group you compare with, the base (27): 11 ÷ 27 = 0.41.
The first group is about 41% higher. Dividing by 38 instead gives 29%, which answers a different question.

steps.title: Training slows the fall, it does not stop it
steps.text:
A 20-year study followed 21 older track athletes who started at about age 50. Even the nine who stayed elite lost VO₂max: 8% in the first 10 years and 15% in the next [[c:pollock]]. Those who cut their training lost 18% and 34%. Maximal heart rate fell by 5–7 beats·min⁻¹ per decade whatever they did.

A review agrees: the fall of about 10% per decade holds in men and women regardless of activity level [[c:hawkins]]. Hard training may cut it by up to half in young and middle-aged men, but not in older men [[c:hawkins-men]]. Holding high-intensity training lasts about a decade at best [[c:hawkins-decade]].

Women seem unable to bring it below 10% per decade, perhaps through [oestrogen](g:oestrogen) [[c:hawkins-women]] (see the menopause lesson).

claims.text: In 21 older track athletes followed for 20 years, VO₂max fell 8% then 15% per decade in those who stayed elite, and 18% then 34% in those who cut training.

evidence.quote: All groups decreased in maximal oxygen uptake at each testing point (H, 8 and 15%; M, 13 and 14%; and L, 18 and 34% from T1 to T2 and T2 to T3, respectively).

claims.text: VO₂max falls about 10% per decade in men and women regardless of activity level.

evidence.quote: Current evidence supports a 10% per decade decline in VO(2max) in men and women regardless of activity level.

claims.text: Long-term high-intensity exercise may cut the VO₂max loss by up to 50% in young and middle-aged men, but not in older men.

evidence.quote: High-intensity exercise may reduce this loss by up to 50% in young and middle-aged men, but not older men, if maintained long term.

claims.text: Keeping up high-intensity training seems limited to about one decade at best and to a select few people.

evidence.quote: maintaining high-intensity training seems limited to approximately one decade at best and to a select few individuals

claims.text: Middle-aged and older women do not appear able to reduce VO₂max loss below 10% per decade, perhaps because of oestrogen status.

evidence.quote: Middle-aged and older women do not appear to be able to reduce loss rates in VO(2max) to less than 10% per decade, which may be related to estrogen status.

steps.title: Faster after 60–70
steps.text:
After about 70 the fall speeds up. In track and field results, decline rates accelerate from around that age [[c:ganse-accel]]. In athletes still competing at 100, the individual decline rate was about 2.5 times as steep as in athletes aged 80–96, steepest in the 100 m sprint [[c:ganse-100]]. These are sprint, jump and throwing events, not endurance, but VO₂max shows the same non-linear pattern: extra loss in people over 70 [[c:hawkins-nl]].

So a straight line fitted through ages 40–60 and extended to 80 flatters the old. [Cross-sectional](g:cross-sectional-study) curves also hide the speed-up, because each age group is a different set of people. Following the same people over time shows it [[c:fleg]].

claims.text: Performance decline rates in athletes accelerate after about age 70.

evidence.quote: While physical performance decline rates accelerate after around the age of 70 years

claims.text: In athletes still competing at 100, the individual decline rate was 2.53 times as steep as in athletes aged 80–96.

evidence.quote: the individual decline rate of the centenarian group was 2.53 times as steep

claims.text: VO₂max loss is not linear: there are non-linear loss rates in people over 70.

evidence.quote: Non-linear loss rates are also demonstrated in individuals over the age of 70 years.

claims.text: In 810 healthy adults followed for a median of 8 years, the loss of VO₂max accelerated with age, to over 20% per decade in the 70s.

evidence.quote: the rate of decline accelerated from 3% to 6% per 10 years in the 20s and 30s to >20% per 10 years in the 70s and beyond

steps.title: How far can you trust this?
steps.text:
Most of this evidence has limits you can name.

- Records and age-group curves are [cross-sectional](g:cross-sectional-study): different people at each age. The few still racing at 75 are [survivors](g:survivorship-bias), fitter than most people of their birth year.
- Lifelong exercisers chose to exercise. Genes, health and drive may differ from non-exercisers, so the gap of 34 against 22 is not all due to training. The study did not randomise anyone to 50 years of training.
- Samples are small: 21 athletes in the 20-year study, 28 lifelong exercisers (7 women).
- Few women run at the oldest ages, so an apparent widening of the sex gap there is confounded [[c:sexconf]].

claims.text: The apparent widening of sex differences in older runners is confounded by the smaller number of older women who compete.

evidence.quote: interpretation of this apparent widening of sex differences with advancing age is confounded by the relatively smaller number of female versus male runners in the older groups

points: Endurance performance holds to about 35, eases until 50–60, then falls faster; the fall is smaller in cycling than in running or swimming.
Lifelong exercisers keep much more VO₂max than non-exercisers of the same age, but stay well below young exercisers.
Even athletes who keep training hard lost 8–15% VO₂max per decade; training slows the fall, it does not stop it.
Decline speeds up after about 70, so a straight-line forecast is too kind to the old.
Records, small samples and self-selection limit what these data show.

variants.stem: Roughly at what age does the fall in peak endurance performance turn from modest to steep?

options.text: From about 25
options.why: VO₂max starts to fall around 25–30, but race performance holds until about 35.

options.text: After about 50–60
options.why: Right: modest decreases from about 35 to 50–60, then progressively steeper.

options.text: Only after about 85
options.why: The steep part starts much earlier, in the 50s or 60s.

options.text: It never turns: the fall is a straight line
options.why: Reviews describe a curve that gets steeper with age.

variants.stem: A 58-year-old triathlete compares times with age 30 in each leg. Which leg has most likely slowed the least?

options.text: Running
options.why: Running shows larger declines than cycling.

options.text: Swimming
options.why: Swimming also falls more than cycling.

options.text: Cycling
options.why: Right: age-related declines are smaller in cycling than in running and swimming.

options.text: All three by the same amount
options.why: The review found the size of the fall depends on the sport.

variants.stem: Men: lifelong exercisers had a VO₂max of 34 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, young exercisers 53. By what percent are the lifelong exercisers below the young?

options.why: That divides by 34 (the wrong base): 19 ÷ 34.
That is the raw difference in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, not a percent.
That is 34 ÷ 53: the share they keep, not how far below they are.

variants.solution: Difference 53 − 34 = 19. Base is the young group: 19 ÷ 53 = 0.358, about 36% below.

variants.stem: Women: lifelong exercisers had a VO₂max of 26 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, young exercisers 44. By what percent are the lifelong exercisers below the young?

options.why: That divides by 26 (the wrong base): 18 ÷ 26.
That is the raw difference, not a percent.
That is 26 ÷ 44: the share they keep.

variants.solution: Difference 44 − 26 = 18. Base is the young group: 18 ÷ 44 = 0.409, about 41% below.

variants.stem: Women: lifelong exercisers had a VO₂max of 26 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, non-exercisers of the same age 18. By what percent are the lifelong exercisers above the non-exercisers?

options.why: That divides by 26 (the wrong base): 8 ÷ 26.
That is the raw difference, not a percent.
That is 26 ÷ 18: how many times as high, not how much higher.

variants.solution: Difference 26 − 18 = 8. Base is the non-exercisers: 8 ÷ 18 = 0.444, about 44% above.

variants.stem: Which sentence fits the lifelong exercisers' results best?

options.text: They kept far more VO₂max than non-exercisers but stayed well below young exercisers
options.why: Right: the middle position, in men and in women.

options.text: Decades of training erased the effect of age on VO₂max
options.why: They were still about 36–41% below the young exercisers.

options.text: Their VO₂max did not differ from non-exercisers; only muscle did
options.why: Their VO₂max was clearly higher: 34 against 22 in men.

options.text: Only the performance-trained group gained over non-exercisers
options.why: Even the fitness group (27) was above non-exercisers (22).

variants.stem: In the 20-year follow-up of older track athletes, how much did VO₂max fall in the first 10 years in the group that stayed elite?

options.text: About 0%: elite training stops the fall
options.why: Even the elite group lost VO₂max at each testing point.

options.text: About 8%
options.why: Right: 8% in the first decade, then 15%.

options.text: About 18%
options.why: That is the loss of the group that greatly reduced training.

options.text: About 34%
options.why: That is the second-decade loss of the group that cut training.

variants.stem: A coach tells a 52-year-old: "Train as hard as at 40 and your VO₂max will still be the same at 70." How well does the evidence back this?

options.text: Poorly: athletes who kept training hard still lost 8–15% per decade
options.why: Right: the 20-year follow-up and the review both show a fall despite hard training.

options.text: Fully: elite training stops the age-related fall
options.why: The elite group lost 8% and then 15% per decade.

options.text: Fully: the fall only happens in women
options.why: The fall of about 10% per decade holds for men and women.

options.text: Not at all: training makes the fall faster
options.why: Training slows the fall; it does not speed it up.

variants.stem: A club fits a straight line to its members' times from age 40 to 60 and uses it to predict times at 80. What is the likely error?

options.text: It will predict times that are too fast, because the fall speeds up after about 70
options.why: Right: decline rates accelerate in the 70s and beyond.

options.text: It will predict times that are too slow, because masters athletes level off
options.why: Decline accelerates; it does not level off.

options.text: No error: the fall is the same every decade
options.why: Reviews describe a non-linear fall.

options.text: It will be right for men but wrong for women
options.why: Both sexes show the acceleration.

variants.stem: A study finds lifelong exercisers aged 74 have a VO₂max of 34, non-exercisers 22. Which limit most weakens the claim "exercise raised VO₂max by 12"?

options.text: People who exercise for 50 years may differ in genes and health
options.why: Right: nobody was randomised, so selection can explain part of the gap.

options.text: VO₂max cannot be measured reliably in people over 70 years old
options.why: It can: the study measured it in a maximal cycle test.

options.text: Muscle capillaries were measured as well as VO₂max in the study
options.why: Extra measurements do not weaken the VO₂max result.

options.text: The lifelong exercisers trained too many hours to be compared
options.why: Training volume is a strength of the design, not a limit on this claim.

variants.stem: Marathon times by age group are plotted from race results. Why can the 75-year-old group look better than the typical 75-year-old runner would have done?

options.text: Older runners are always faster than the curve predicts
options.why: There is no such rule.

options.text: Race results are measured in different units by age
options.why: Times are measured the same way at every age.

options.text: Only the fit and healthy 75-year-olds still enter races
options.why: Right: survivorship bias, since people who stopped through injury or illness are missing.

options.text: Younger runners train less than older runners
options.why: Nothing in the data suggests so.
